summary: A report on the second Network Graphics Group meeting at Stanford's AI lab. It covers experiment reports, talks about how graphics connections should work and whether to use one protocol for all display types, and the drafting of a first-pass graphics protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC reports on a Network Graphics Group meeting at Stanford. Attendees reviewed experiments, considered how graphics systems should connect, and agreed on initial assumptions for a drawing protocol.

subtitle: Meeting notes on graphics experiments and a first-pass network graphics protocol.

tldr.problem: Attendees were exploring how to connect graphics systems and describe pictures across hosts and different display types.
tldr.mechanism: The meeting reviewed experiments, discussed connection models and agreed on assumptions and low-level operators for a first-pass output protocol.
tldr.outcome: Committees were assigned to draft connection and output protocols; the RFC records discussions and agreements, not a completed standard.

sections.title: Meeting Questions and Agreement
sections.content:
The second Network Graphics Group meeting was convened at the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab on November 21. Its agenda covered experiment reports, prepared talks and specification of a first-pass graphics protocol.

Early discussion focused on how graphics connections should be established and whether static and interactive devices needed separate protocols. An apparent consensus favored a single protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The group discussed how graphics devices should connect and whether one protocol could serve different display types. The meeting notes report an apparent preference for one protocol.

sections.title: Reports from Experiments
sections.content:
The RAND-UCSB experiment using OLS from Rand graphics terminals was reported as successful. Larger Host-to-Host allocations produced smoother drawing in the demonstration; at minimum allocation, NCP-NCP overhead made the picture appear a portion at a time.

Other reports described partial progress or obstacles: an SDC-DMCG tablet-input experiment transmitted some data, an Illinois-Multics experiment was prevented by an NCP bug and machine switch, and the SEX-NIC experiment had not yet been performed. Attendees said network host reliability could hamper graphics work but was not crippling.
sections.plainLanguage: One graphics experiment worked, while others met hardware, software or availability problems. Attendees said host reliability could make graphics work harder.

sections.title: Connections and Processing Locations
sections.content:
Attendees discussed using TELNET for simple graphics and an additional socket pair for complex graphics that use an intermediate form. They identified simple, smart and powerful graphics devices, and considered whether application, graphics and device-conversion work might run at the device, local host or remote host.

A committee was assigned to formulate a Graphics Connection Protocol. The meeting's consensus was that only device-specific codes should pass over TELNET connections unless the committee found a compelling reason otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: Graphics work could happen on the display, the nearby computer or a remote host. A committee was asked to define how a graphics connection should be set up.

sections.title: First-Pass Output Assumptions
sections.content:
The agreed assumptions include a virtual screen with its origin at the center, signed two's-complement fractional coordinates from -.5 to +.499, and an initial Standard Graphics Stream of 8-bit bytes with two-byte coordinates. Text output uses Network ASCII.

The protocol is organized by complexity: level 0 for simple drawing, level 1 for one level of subpicture definitions, and level 2 for viewport and window operators. Operators discussed include erase, move, draw, point, line type, line intensity, text and escape. The protocol committee was to prioritize output before input.
sections.plainLanguage: The group agreed on an initial coordinate system and a small set of drawing commands. It planned to develop output rules first, with input recommendations as a later priority.
